messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Librarian
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mai sits in the waiting room, tracing the pattern on the carpet with her eyes. For the past eighteen months, her world has been shrinking, and it was a moment in the place she once loved most—the library—that finally made her pick up the phone. Mai is 52, and for twenty of those years, the hushed halls of the public library were her sanctuary. Now, they are a minefield. The trouble began the night the hurricane made landfall. She and her husband, Bao, had huddled in the basement with two other families from their block. She remembers the roar of the wind, a physical pressure that seemed to squeeze the air from her lungs. But what haunts her most isn't the noise; it's the moment it stopped. After hours of shrieking wind and the percussive slam of debris against the house, an absolute, deafening silence fell. In that quiet, before the sirens began, came the terrifying certainty that they were the only ones left, that everything outside their basement had been erased. When she allows the memory to surface, or more accurately, when it forces its way into her mind uninvited, it is this silence, and the profound, bottomless grief for her ruined neighborhood that follows, that overwhelms her.

In the months that followed, Mai found that the world was full of reminders. The most potent, paradoxically, was quiet. At work, the gentle hum of the library would occasionally dip into true silence—perhaps between patron requests or after a children's story hour concluded. In these moments, without warning, she would be right back in the basement, the smell of damp concrete in her nose, her heart hammering against her ribs. She learned to fight it by deliberately trying to leave her body, focusing on the scuff on her shoe or the grain of the wood on her desk until her mind felt fuzzy and distant, a strategy that left her feeling foggy and disconnected for hours. Nighttime became another source of dread. Waking up in the dark was like waking up in the storm again, the power gone, the world outside an unknown and hostile place. She insisted on a nightlight, much to Bao’s confusion, and found herself avoiding going to bed until she was utterly exhausted.

Her daily routines became a series of careful calculations aimed at feeling safe. She stopped her morning walks because the sensation of her own heart beating hard in her chest felt too much like the terror of the storm. At work, she would only sit in the staff room chair that was tucked into the corner, giving her a clear view of the door and no unseen space behind her. She found herself constantly scanning the faces of patrons, checking the windows, always on guard for a danger she couldn't name. This hypervigilance was exhausting, a low-level hum of anxiety that never fully ceased. The avoidance extended beyond places and into people. Seeing her old neighbors, the very ones she had sheltered with, became unbearable. A chance encounter with Mrs. Tran in the produce aisle sent a jolt of panic through her, the sight of the woman’s face instantly bringing back the memory of their shared helplessness. Mai began changing her grocery shopping schedule, isolating herself from the very community that had survived alongside her.

The breaking point came last Tuesday. She was re-shelving books in the quiet history section when the memory ambushed her. One moment she was holding a biography of Lincoln, the next she was on the floor, crouched between the stacks, tears streaming down her face, overwhelmed by a grief so total it felt like drowning. A colleague found her, and the gentle concern in the young woman’s eyes was mixed with an alarm that filled Mai with a deep sense of shame. She had come to believe that this was a permanent break inside her, a weakness she had to hide. But now, sitting in this quiet office, she is holding onto a fragile hope that she might one day be able to sit in silence again and feel not terror, but peace.
